lessons.title: Brainstorming Techniques for New Business Ideas
lessons.body:
To generate business ideas, you don't need a genius momentâyou need a method. Start with the 'Problem Flood' technique. For one week, carry a small notebook or use a free app like Google Keep. Write down every frustration you see or experience: the long queue at the water point, the boda boda that overcharges, the maize flour that spoils quickly. Aim for 20 problems. Then, pick the top 5 that you or people you know face daily. For each, ask: 'How could I solve this with what I have?' This is the seed of a business.

Next, use 'SCAMPER' to twist existing products. SCAMPER stands for Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse. For example, a woman in Kenya sold mandazi (fried dough). She substituted wheat flour with cassava flour (Substitute), reducing cost by 40%. She combined mandazi with a delivery service for offices (Combine). You can do the same with any local product. Write each SCAMPER letter and force 3 ideas per letter. That's 21 ideas in 30 minutes.

Another powerful technique is 'Brainstorming Circles'. Gather 5-6 friends or fellow traders. Sit in a circle. One person states a problem, e.g., 'Farmers lose tomatoes after harvest.' Each person gives one idea, no matter how wild. No criticism allowed. Write all ideas on a flipchart or a wall using sticky notes. After 15 minutes, you'll have 30-50 ideas. Then vote for the top 3. This method works because it taps into collective knowledge and reduces fear of judgment.

Finally, use 'Observation Walks'. Visit a busy market like Balogun in Lagos or Kariakoo in Dar es Salaam. Spend one hour watching what people buy, what they complain about, and what they carry. Note gaps: Is there no clean drinking water? No phone charging station? No affordable lunch? Each gap is a potential business. Combine these techniques weekly. Keep an 'Idea Journal'. Review it monthly. You'll soon have more ideas than you can pursue.

lessons.title: Evaluating Market Gaps and Unmet Needs
lessons.body:
A market gap is a need that customers have but no one is satisfying well. To find one, look for three things: high demand, poor supply, and willingness to pay. Start by counting. Visit a market and count how many vendors sell a product, say, mobile phone accessories. If there are 10 vendors and 200 customers per day, the market is crowded. But if you see 10 vendors and they all run out of phone chargers by noon, that's a gap. In Kigali, a young man noticed that hardware stores sold paint but no one offered color mixing. He started a paint-mixing service and now supplies 30 contractors.

Use the '5 Whys' to dig deeper. Ask 'Why?' five times about a problem. Example: Why do farmers in Uganda get low prices for maize? Because they sell immediately after harvest. Why? Because they need cash. Why? Because they have no storage. Why? Because storage costs money. Why? Because banks won't lend to small farmers. The gap: affordable storage or a loan product. Your business could be a small warehouse or a mobile money-based savings group.

Check demand with simple tools. Use Google Trends (free) to see if searches for a product are rising. In Nigeria, searches for 'solar inverter' grew 200% from 2020 to 2023. That's a gap. Also, talk to at least 20 potential customers. Ask: 'What do you currently do when you need X?' and 'How much do you pay?' If they already pay for a poor solution, they'll pay for a better one. For example, women in Ghana paid 5 cedis for a bucket of water from vendors. A new borehole with a small fee of 2 cedis per bucket would be a gap.

Finally, look for 'underserved' groups: rural areas, low-income earners, women, and youth. A gap exists if a group is ignored by big companies. In Ethiopia, injera (flatbread) is made at home, but working women have no time. A business that delivers fresh injera batter daily fills a gap. Always verify: Can you reach these customers? Can they afford your price? If yes, you've found a real opportunity.

lessons.title: Conducting Customer Discovery Interviews
lessons.body:
Customer discovery interviews are conversations to learn what customers actually need, not to sell. The goal is to understand their problems, current solutions, and spending. Do at least 20 interviews before building anything. Start with people you know, then ask for referrals. Go where they are: markets, bus parks, churches, mosques, or online via WhatsApp groups. Use a simple notebook or a free app like Otter.ai to record (with permission).

Ask open-ended questions. Never ask 'Would you buy this?' because people lie to be polite. Instead, ask: 'Tell me about the last time you needed [product/service]. What did you do?' 'What was the hardest part?' 'How much did you spend?' 'What did you like or dislike about the solution you used?' For example, if you're thinking of a laundry service, ask: 'How do you currently wash your clothes? How long does it take? What do you do when you're busy?' Listen for emotionsâfrustration, anger, or relief. Those signal a real problem.

Avoid pitching your idea. If you mention your solution, the customer will focus on being nice. Instead, keep the conversation about them. Take notes on exact words. If 15 out of 20 people say 'I hate queuing at the bank,' that's a pattern. If only 2 say it, it's not a big enough problem. Also, ask about their budget: 'How much do you spend on this per week?' If they spend 500 naira on phone charging, a solar charging business could charge 200 naira and still profit.

After 20 interviews, look for patterns. Group answers into themes: price, convenience, quality, trust. The theme that appears most is your opportunity. For instance, a entrepreneur in Tanzania interviewed 25 small shop owners. 20 said they lost sales because they ran out of airtime. He started a mobile airtime delivery service and now serves 100 shops. Remember: interviews are not about confirming your idea; they are about discovering the truth. Be ready to change your idea based on what you hear.

lessons.title: Validating Problem-Solution Fit
lessons.body:
Problem-solution fit means you have evidence that your solution solves a problem people care about and will pay for. It's not about a perfect product; it's about a minimum viable product (MVP) that tests your assumptions. Start by writing down your top 3 assumptions: e.g., 'Customers will pay 1000 naira for home delivery,' 'Farmers will use a mobile app to sell produce,' 'People will buy pre-cooked beans.' Then design a simple test for each.

One low-cost test is the 'Landing Page' test. Use free tools like Carrd or Google Forms to create a one-page description of your service with a 'Buy Now' or 'Register Interest' button. Share the link on WhatsApp, Facebook, or local groups. If 100 people visit and 10 click 'Buy,' that's a 10% conversionâa good sign. If no one clicks, your solution may not fit. Another test is 'Pre-Sales.' For example, if you want to sell packaged garri, take orders and deposits before you buy packaging. If 20 people pay 500 naira deposit, you have validation.

For physical products, do a 'Pop-Up Stall.' Set up a small table at a market or outside a church. Sell a small batch. Watch how people react. Do they ask questions? Do they buy? Do they come back? In Accra, a woman tested a new spice mix by selling at a bus station. She sold 50 packs in 2 hours. That's validation. If she sold only 5, she would know to change the recipe or price.

Also, track 'Problem Frequency.' Ask customers how often they face the problem. If it's daily, they need a daily solution. If it's once a year, it's a hard business. For example, a plumber is needed when pipes burstârare but urgent. A food vendor is needed daily. Choose problems that occur at least weekly. Finally, measure 'Willingness to Pay.' If customers say they'll pay but don't, it's not validation. Only money or a signed commitment counts. Once you have 10 paying customers, you have problem-solution fit. Then you can scale.

lessons.title: Assessing Feasibility: Technical, Financial, and Legal
lessons.body:
Before you invest money, check if your idea is feasible in three areas: technical, financial, and legal. Technical feasibility asks: Can you actually make or deliver this? Do you have the skills, equipment, and suppliers? For example, if you want to start a bakery, do you know how to bake? Do you have an oven? Can you get flour at a good price? If not, you need training or a partner. In Kenya, a group of youth wanted to make solar panels but lacked the technical know-how. They switched to assembling solar lamps from imported kitsâmuch easier. Write a list of every step from raw material to customer. Identify any step you can't do. That's a red flag.

Financial feasibility means the numbers work. Calculate your start-up costs: equipment, rent, licenses, initial stock. Then estimate monthly costs: materials, transport, salaries, airtime. Estimate your selling price and how many units you can sell per month. Use a simple formula: Break-even = Fixed Costs / (Price - Variable Cost per Unit). For example, if your fixed costs are 50,000 naira per month, price is 500 naira, and variable cost is 300 naira, then break-even = 50,000 / (500-300) = 250 units per month. Can you sell 250? If not, the idea is not financially feasible. Also, check if you can get a loan or grant. In Nigeria, you can apply for a BOI (Bank of Industry) loan or a Tony Elumelu Foundation grant.

Legal feasibility is about rules. Do you need a business registration? In most African countries, you can register a business name for as low as 5,000 naira (Nigeria) or 1,000 shillings (Kenya). Some businesses need special licenses: food handling, health permits, import/export. For example, selling bottled water requires a NAFDAC number in Nigeria. Selling alcohol requires a liquor license. If you ignore these, you risk fines or shutdown. Also, check local bylaws: can you run a business from home? Do you need a permit for a market stall? Visit your local government office or ask other traders. Spend one day researching. It's better to know now than to be closed later.

lessons.title: Workshop: Generating and Screening Business Ideas
lessons.body:
This workshop brings together all the techniques from this module. You will generate 20 business ideas, then screen them to find the top 3. Set aside 2 hours. You need a pen, paper, and a timer. Work alone or with a small group. Step 1: Idea Generation (30 minutes). Use three methods: (a) Problem Flood: write 10 problems you see daily. (b) SCAMPER: pick one local product and apply each letter to create 7 variations. (c) Observation Walk: recall a recent market visit and list 3 gaps. Combine all into a master list of 20 ideas. Don't judge yet.

Step 2: Quick Screen (20 minutes). For each idea, ask three yes/no questions: (1) Can I start this with less than 50,000 naira (or equivalent)? (2) Do I have or can I quickly learn the basic skill? (3) Is there evidence that people will pay for it? If an idea gets three 'yes', keep it. If two 'yes', keep it as maybe. If one or zero, drop it. This should reduce your list to 5-8 ideas.

Step 3: Deep Screen (40 minutes). For each remaining idea, do a mini-feasibility check. Write: Target customer, Problem solved, Your solution, Price, Cost per unit, Break-even units per month. Then score each idea from 1 to 5 on: Market demand (how many people need it?), Competition (is it crowded?), Your passion (do you like it?), and Profit potential (can you make 30% margin?). Add the scores. The idea with the highest total is your best bet. For example, in a workshop in Kampala, a participant had 20 ideas. After screening, the top idea was 'mobile phone repair and charging kiosk' because demand was high, competition was low in her area, and she already knew how to repair.

Step 4: Action Plan (30 minutes). For your top idea, write the next 3 steps you will take this week: e.g., 'Interview 5 potential customers,' 'Find a supplier for phone screens,' 'Calculate exact start-up costs.' Set a deadline. Share your plan with a friend who will hold you accountable. Remember, an idea is worthless without action. This workshop gives you a clear path from idea to opportunity. Repeat it every month to keep your pipeline full.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Idea Generation and Opportunity Recognition for African Agribusiness

This practical reference consolidates the core tools, frameworks, and field-tested practices from the module Idea Generation and Opportunity Recognition. It is written for African entrepreneurs, cooperative leaders, extension officers, and SME owners who want to move from a vague business idea to a validated, feasible opportunity. Every section is business-first: what you do, what it costs, what can go wrong, and how to measure progress.

Across Africa, the agribusiness opportunity space is enormous but fragmented. Demand for processed foods, cold-chain logistics, inputs, aggregation, and digital advisory services is growing faster than supply in many value chains. Yet most new ventures fail not because the idea was bad, but because the founder never validated the problem, never tested willingness to pay, or ignored regulatory and financing realities. This reference gives you the practical sequence to avoid those failures.

1. Brainstorming Techniques for New Business Ideas

Good brainstorming in African agribusiness is not random. It is structured around assets you already have access to: land, relationships, local knowledge, cooperative membership, or a distribution route. Use these four techniques:

  • Value chain mapping: Walk one commodity from farm to fork (e.g., cassava, poultry, mango). Mark every point where value is lost or where a middleman takes a margin. Each gap is a business idea.
  • Problem inventory: List 20 problems farmers, traders, or consumers complain about weekly. Rank by frequency and pain intensity.
  • SCAMPER: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse. Example: combine mobile money with input retail to solve payment trust.
  • Cross-sector borrowing: Take a model that works elsewhere (e.g., boda-boda delivery) and apply it to cold-chain or feed distribution.

2. Evaluating Market Gaps and Unmet Needs

A market gap exists when demand is real, recurring, and currently underserved. In African markets, gaps often hide in plain sight: inconsistent quality, unpredictable supply, lack of grading, no cold chain, no credit, or no reliable information. Score each candidate gap on the matrix below before spending money.

Table 1: Market Gap Screening Matrix (score 1â5; 5 = strongest)
Criterion What to ask Weight
Demand frequencyDo customers buy weekly/monthly or once?Ã3
Willingness to payHave they paid for a similar solution before?Ã3
Competition intensityHow many alternatives exist and how good are they?Ã2
Access to customersCan you reach them through existing channels?Ã2
Your capability fitDo you have skills, network, or assets?Ã2
Regulatory easeLicences, permits, standards required?Ã1
Source: Adapted from ILO Start and Improve Your Business (SIYB) market assessment tools and the FAO Agribusiness Planning guidelines.

3. Conducting Customer Discovery Interviews

Customer discovery is not selling. It is listening. In African agribusiness, interviews must be done in the customer's environment: at the farm gate, in the market stall, at the mill, or at the input shop. Aim for 15â30 interviews per segment. Ask about past behaviour, not future intentions.

Good questions: "Walk me through how you bought your last bag of fertilizer." "What went wrong the last time?" "How much did you spend?" "What did you do when the product was unavailable?"

Bad questions: "Would you buy this?" "Do you think this is a good idea?" These produce polite lies, not data.

Table 2: Customer Discovery Interview Log (sample structure)
Date Customer type Problem stated Current workaround Spend (local currency) Signal (strong/weak)
12/03Maize farmer, 2 haFake inputsBuys from known agrodealerKES 18,000/seasonStrong
14/03Poultry traderNo cold storageSells same day at low priceKES 5,000/week lossStrong
15/03Urban restaurantInconsistent supplyMultiple suppliersKES 40,000/monthMedium
18/03Cooperative managerNo aggregation dataPaper recordsKES 0 (no budget)Weak
Source: Structure adapted from The Mom Test by Rob Fitzpatrick and the USAID Feed the Future market systems development guidance.

4. Validating ProblemâSolution Fit

Problemâsolution fit exists when your target customer confirms the problem is painful, frequent, and currently unsolved in a satisfactory way, and your proposed solution directly addresses it. In African agribusiness, validate with three tests:

  1. Payment test: Ask for a deposit, pre-order, or signed commitment. Verbal enthusiasm is not validation.
  2. Repeat test: Run a small pilot. Do customers come back without prompting?
  3. Referral test: Do customers refer others without incentive? This signals real value in trust-based markets.

If fewer than 40% of interviewed customers show a strong signal (documented spend, workaround cost, or repeat purchase), return to idea generation. Do not scale a weak signal.

5. Assessing Feasibility: Technical, Financial, and Legal

Feasibility assessment is where many African agribusiness ideas die â and that is a good thing if it happens before you invest savings. Assess three dimensions in parallel:

  • Technical: Can you produce or deliver at the required quality, volume, and consistency? Do you have access to raw materials, equipment, skills, and maintenance? Consider climate, seasonality, and post-harvest loss.
  • Financial: Calculate unit economics: cost per unit, price per unit, gross margin, break-even volume, and cash conversion cycle. In African markets, cash flow timing matters more than profit margin. Many profitable businesses fail because they run out of working capital during the lean season.
  • Legal: Business registration, tax obligations, sector licences (e.g., seed certification, food safety, veterinary permits), land tenure, and contract enforceability. Requirements vary by country and county/district.
â  SAFETY AND COMPLIANCE WARNING

Do not sell, distribute, or process agricultural inputs, seeds, veterinary drugs, or food products without the required national licences and standards certification. Unregistered agrochemicals, counterfeit seeds, and unlicensed food processing are illegal in most African countries, expose customers to health and crop failure risks, and can result in fines, closure, or criminal liability. Always verify requirements with your national agriculture ministry, bureau of standards, and local government before piloting. When handling chemicals or operating processing equipment, follow manufacturer safety instructions and provide protective equipment to workers.

6. Workshop: Generating and Screening Business Ideas

Run this 3-hour workshop with your team, cooperative, or incubator cohort. It works with 5â30 participants.

  1. Warm-up (15 min): Each participant names one problem they saw in the last week in their value chain.
  2. Divergent generation (30 min): Use value chain mapping and SCAMPER. Target 20+ ideas. No criticism allowed.
  3. Clustering (20 min): Group ideas by customer segment and value chain stage.
  4. Screening (40 min): Score each cluster using Table 1. Keep the top 3.
  5. Discovery planning (45 min): For each of the top 3, write 10 interview questions and identify 10 customers to interview within 7 days.
  6. Feasibility snapshot (30 min): For each idea, list the biggest technical, financial, and legal risk.
  7. Commitment (20 min): Each team commits to completing 15 interviews before the next session.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â I generated at least 20 ideas before selecting one.
  • â I scored my top ideas against demand, willingness to pay, competition, and capability.
  • â I interviewed 15â30 real customers in their own environment.
  • â I asked about past behaviour and spend, not future intentions.
  • â At least 40% of interviewees showed a strong problem signal.
  • â I tested willingness to pay with a deposit, pre-order, or pilot purchase.
  • â I assessed technical, financial, and legal feasibility before investing.
  • â I confirmed all required licences and standards with the relevant authority.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • ILO Start and Improve Your Business (SIYB) â free business planning and market assessment tools used across Africa.
  • FAO Sustainable Food Value Chains â practical guides on value chain analysis and agribusiness development.
  • USAID Feed the Future â market systems development and enterprise development resources.
  • AgriProFocus â African agribusiness networks, toolkits, and country-specific guides.
  • African Development Bank â Enable Youth Africa â agribusiness entrepreneurship support and financing information.

This practical reference is part of the Rise Africa Skills Entrepreneurship course. Use it alongside the workshop and field assignments to move from idea to validated, feasible, and legally compliant agribusiness opportunity.

quiz.q: What is the 'Problem Flood' technique?
options: A) Writing down every frustration you see or experience for a week
B) Flooding social media with your business idea
C) Asking friends to give you money for your idea
D) Copying a competitor's business exactly
quiz.explanation: Problem Flood involves noting daily problems to find business ideas.

quiz.q: What does the 'S' in SCAMPER stand for?
quiz.explanation: SCAMPER stands for Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse.

quiz.q: In Brainstorming Circles, what is the main rule?
options: A) Only the leader can speak
C) Each person must give 10 ideas
quiz.explanation: No criticism encourages free flow of ideas without fear.

quiz.q: What is an 'Observation Walk'?
options: A) Walking to exercise while thinking
B) Visiting a market to watch what people buy and complain about
C) Walking around your house looking for ideas
D) A walk to meet investors
quiz.explanation: Observation Walks involve watching market behavior to spot gaps.

quiz.q: How many ideas should you aim to generate in a Brainstorming Circle in 15 minutes?
quiz.explanation: With 5-6 people giving one idea each per round, you can get 30-50 ideas quickly.

quiz.q: What are the three signs of a market gap?
options: A) High demand, poor supply, willingness to pay
B) Low demand, high supply, no payment
C) Many competitors, low prices, high costs
D) Government subsidies, free products, low interest
quiz.explanation: A gap exists when demand is high, supply is poor, and customers will pay.

quiz.q: What is the '5 Whys' technique used for?
options: A) To ask five customers for feedback
B) To dig deeper into the root cause of a problem
C) To generate five business ideas
quiz.explanation: Asking 'Why?' five times helps uncover the root cause of a problem.

quiz.q: Which free tool can show if searches for a product are rising?
quiz.explanation: Google Trends shows search interest over time for any term.

quiz.q: What is an underserved group in market gap analysis?
options: A) People who have many options
B) Rural areas, low-income earners, women, and youth
quiz.explanation: These groups are often ignored by big companies, creating opportunities.

quiz.q: How many customer discovery interviews should you do before building anything?
quiz.explanation: At least 20 interviews help identify patterns and real needs.

quiz.q: What is a bad question to ask in a customer discovery interview?
options: A) 'Tell me about the last time you needed this.'
quiz.explanation: 'Would you buy this?' leads to polite lies; focus on past behavior.

quiz.q: What should you listen for in customer interviews?
options: B) Emotions like frustration or anger
quiz.explanation: Emotions signal a real problem that needs solving.

quiz.q: What is a good pattern to look for after 20 interviews?
options: A) If 2 out of 20 mention a problem
B) If 15 out of 20 mention the same problem
quiz.explanation: A majority mentioning the same problem indicates a significant opportunity.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid pitching your idea during customer discovery?
options: B) It makes customers focus on being nice instead of honest
quiz.explanation: Pitching leads to biased feedback; you want the truth about their problems.

quiz.q: What is a minimum viable product (MVP)?
options: A) The final version of your product
B) A simple version to test assumptions
C) A product that costs the least
D) A product with no features
quiz.explanation: An MVP tests key assumptions with minimal resources.

quiz.q: What is a Landing Page test?
options: A) A physical page in a book
B) A one-page website to measure interest
C) A page in a newspaper
D) A test on an airplane
quiz.explanation: A landing page with a call-to-action measures real interest.

quiz.q: What is a good conversion rate for a landing page test?
quiz.explanation: 10% click-through or sign-up is a strong signal of problem-solution fit.

quiz.q: What is pre-sales validation?
options: A) Selling before you have the product
quiz.explanation: Taking deposits before production proves customers will pay.

quiz.q: What does 'problem frequency' refer to?
options: A) How often the problem occurs
B) How loud the problem is
C) How many people have the problem
D) How much the problem costs
quiz.explanation: Problems that occur daily or weekly are better for business than rare ones.

quiz.q: What is the only true validation of problem-solution fit?
options: A) Friends saying they like it
B) Money or a signed commitment
D) Many likes on social media
quiz.explanation: Only paying customers or firm commitments prove real demand.

quiz.q: What does technical feasibility assess?
options: A) Can you make or deliver the product?
B) Can you get a loan?
quiz.explanation: Technical feasibility checks skills, equipment, and suppliers.

quiz.q: What is the break-even formula?
options: A) Fixed Costs / (Price - Variable Cost per Unit)
quiz.explanation: Break-even units = Fixed Costs divided by contribution margin per unit.

quiz.q: If fixed costs are 50,000 naira, price is 500 naira, and variable cost is 300 naira, what is the break-even quantity?
Why is legal feasibility important?
options: A) To avoid fines or shutdown
quiz.explanation: Ignoring licenses and regulations can lead to fines or business closure.

quiz.q: In Nigeria, what is required to sell bottled water?
quiz.explanation: NAFDAC regulates food and drugs, including bottled water.

quiz.q: In the workshop, how many business ideas should you generate first?
quiz.explanation: The workshop starts with generating 20 ideas before screening.

quiz.q: In the quick screen, how many 'yes' answers keep an idea?
quiz.explanation: Three 'yes' answers (low start-up cost, skill, evidence of payment) keep the idea.

quiz.q: What are the four criteria for deep screening?
options: A) Market demand, competition, passion, profit potential
quiz.explanation: These four factors help rank ideas objectively.

quiz.q: What should you do after selecting your top idea in the workshop?
options: B) Write next 3 steps and set a deadline
D) Borrow a lot of money
quiz.explanation: An action plan with deadlines turns an idea into reality.

quiz.q: How often should you repeat the workshop?
quiz.explanation: Monthly repetition keeps your pipeline of ideas fresh.
